pos: n. (the designation of Hepher, one of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Mekerathi, of Mecherah, a place otherwise unknown; named once, 1 Chronicles 11:36.
biblical_def: Mecherathite is the designation attached to Hepher in the roll of David's mighty men: “Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite” (1 Chronicles 11:36). It means a man of Mecherah, and Mecherah appears nowhere in Scripture; the town is known only through this one man's title. The list it stands in is the muster of the heroes who came to David and made him king over all Israel, and the Chronicler is careful to name each man by his home: the Tahmonite, the Ahohite, the Harodite, the Pelonite, the Gilonite, the Carmelite, the Hittite. These labels are the record's way of showing that David's strength was drawn out of every quarter of the land and from beyond it, Uriah the Hittite among them. “Also the valiant men of the armies were, Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem” (1 Chronicles 11:26) begins the longer catalogue in which Hepher stands. The Mecherathite performed no recorded exploit. He is named, placed, and numbered with the men who held the kingdom together, and his town is remembered only because he came from it.

corruption_summary: Lists of fighting men are read as nationalist myth-making; the Chronicler names each man's town to show the kingdom was gathered, not seized.
corruption_paragraphs: The roll of David's mighty men is often handled as heroic legend attached to a founder-king. The detail of the list argues against it. A composer of legends names champions; a keeper of muster rolls names a man and the obscure village he came from, including villages no one can now locate, and admits foreigners into the company. Hepher the Mecherathite is useless to a propagandist and indispensable to a register.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God builds His kingdom out of named men from particular places. David did not raise a faceless army; the Chronicler says these strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and then lists them one by one. The church is gathered the same way, and the Lamb's book of life is a register, not a census estimate.

pos: n. (the designation of Jasiel, the last of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Metsobayah, of Zobah, or of Mesobah, a place otherwise unidentified; named once, 1 Chronicles 11:47.
biblical_def: Mesobaite is the title of the very last man in the roll of David's mighty men: “Eliel, and Obed, and Jasiel the Mesobaite” (1 Chronicles 11:47). The list closes on him. His home is not identified with certainty; the name is read by some as of Zobah, the Syrian kingdom David subdued, which would make Jasiel another of the foreign-born men in Israel's army, as Uriah the Hittite and Zelek the Ammonite were. Nothing is recorded of his deeds. The chapter opened with the three who broke through the host of the Philistines to draw water out of the well of Bethlehem, and it ends here, with a name and a place and no story. That shape is itself instructive: the Chronicler gives the famous feats first and then the long tail of men who simply served and were counted. “These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom” (1 Chronicles 11:10) governs the whole roll. Jasiel the Mesobaite strengthened himself with David, and Scripture closes the muster with his name.

corruption_summary: Foreigners in Israel's armies are cited as evidence that the covenant had no boundaries; Scripture shows Gentiles joining a kingdom on its own terms, not dissolving it.
corruption_paragraphs: David's roll contains a Hittite, an Ammonite, a Moabite, and probably a Syrian, and this is sometimes used to argue that Israel's covenant distinctives were a late and artificial imposition. The texts read otherwise. Foreigners were received into Israel throughout its history — Rahab, Ruth, Uriah, Ittai the Gittite — by submission to Israel's God and Israel's king, not by Israel's abandoning what made it Israel. The door was open and it had a threshold.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the ingathering of the nations was always the plan and never a loosening of the terms. “Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the LORD, speak, saying, The LORD hath utterly separated me from his people” stands in Isaiah 56, and Jasiel the Mesobaite stands at the end of David's list. The Gentile is admitted by grace through faith, into a kingdom whose King he confesses.

pos: n. (the designation of Eliel, one of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Machavim, of uncertain sense; the place Mahavah is not elsewhere named; named once, 1 Chronicles 11:46.
biblical_def: Mahavite is the designation of one of two men named Eliel in the same roll: “Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite” (1 Chronicles 11:46). The epithet distinguishes him from the Eliel of the next verse, and that is very nearly its whole function in the text. Mahavah itself is unknown; no place of that name occurs anywhere in Scripture, and the Hebrew form is obscure enough that the older lexicographers could not settle it. The verse around him is a good picture of David's company: two brothers listed as the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah a Moabite, standing in Israel's army though Moab was the nation Israel had been forbidden to seek peace with. The muster roll of 1 Chronicles 11 closes a chapter that began with all Israel gathering to David at Hebron and saying, Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh. Eliel the Mahavite is one of the men who made that confession good with his body. His exploits are not recorded; his name, his father's house, and the town nobody can find are.

corruption_summary: Repeated names in the registers are called scribal confusion; the text supplies a distinguishing epithet precisely so the two men are not confused.
corruption_paragraphs: Two men named Eliel appear in consecutive verses of the same list, and the first is marked the Mahavite. Critical handling of such places tends to assume duplication or corruption in transmission. The simpler reading is the one the text invites: the register distinguishes them because they were two men, and it does so by the ordinary means of naming the one by his town. That is what a careful record looks like when two soldiers share a name.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture distinguishes persons God does not confuse. A dictionary that defines one entity twice does its readers an injury, and so would a chronicle that merged two of David's men into one. The LORD knoweth them that are His, individually and by name, and the registers He preserved reflect that care.

pos: n. (the designation of Shephatiah, one of the Benjamites who came to David at Ziklag)
etymology: Hebrew Charuphi, of Haruph, or of Hariph, a family of the return; named once, 1 Chronicles 12:5.
biblical_def: Haruphite is the designation of Shephatiah in the list of the men who joined David while he was still an outlaw: “Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite” (1 Chronicles 12:5). The setting is given at the head of the chapter: “Now these are they that came to David to Ziklag, while he yet kept himself close because of Saul the son of Kish: and they were among the mighty men, helpers of the war” (1 Chronicles 12:1). This is the costly list. These men did not come to David at Hebron when the kingdom was secure; they came to Ziklag while Saul reigned and David was hunted, and they were Benjamites — Saul's own tribe, kinsmen of the king they were leaving. To be named here is to be named among those who chose the anointed of the LORD over the standing power and over their own blood. Shephatiah the Haruphite did that. Nothing else of him is recorded, and the town or family called Haruph is otherwise unknown, though a family of Hariph returned from the captivity centuries later. He is a man identified by a place we cannot find, who made the decision the chapter exists to honour.

corruption_summary: Loyalty is treated as a function of tribe and interest; the Benjamites at Ziklag left their own king's tribe for the man God had anointed.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern political reading of such a list is that men follow their faction. First Chronicles 12 records the opposite: archers of Benjamin, who could use both the right hand and the left, abandoned the house of Saul while Saul still held the throne, and came to a fugitive at Ziklag. The chapter even preserves the oath Amasai spoke when the Spirit came upon him — Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse — which is a confession of divine appointment, not a calculation of advantage.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD's anointing settles allegiance before the throne is secured. The men of Ziklag are the pattern of faith: they committed themselves to a king whose kingdom was not yet visible. The believer does the same with the greater David, confessing a reign the world does not yet see.

pos: n. (the designation of Shamhuth, fifth captain of David's monthly courses)
etymology: Hebrew Yizrach, he will shine forth, from zarach, to rise or to shine, as the sun; named once, 1 Chronicles 27:8.
biblical_def: Izrahite is the designation of the officer set over the fifth of David's twelve monthly divisions: “The fifth captain for the fifth month was Shamhuth the Izrahite: and in his course were twenty and four thousand” (1 Chronicles 27:8). The system is described at the head of the chapter: the chief fathers and captains of thousands and hundreds served the king by rotation, each course coming in and going out month by month throughout the year, and each numbering twenty and four thousand men. It is a standing militia of two hundred eighty-eight thousand, organised so that no part of the nation carried the burden all year and the kingdom was never without an army. Shamhuth's title means one who shines forth, or belonging to a man named Izrah. Nothing is recorded of him beyond his month and his number. The arrangement is the point: David left Israel an ordered kingdom, with the Levites in courses, the singers in courses, the porters in courses, and the army in courses. Order in the house of God and order in the realm came from the same hand, and the New Testament keeps the principle: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

corruption_summary: Order in church and state is dismissed as institutional coldness; David's courses show order as the form love takes when a people must be governed.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of modern religion treats structure as the enemy of life, and the result in practice is congregations without officers, worship without pattern, and ministry without accountability. First Chronicles 27 is one of several chapters recording the courses David established for the army, the priesthood, the singers and the gatekeepers, and Scripture presents these arrangements as a blessing to the nation, not a burden on it. Twenty-four thousand men served one month and went home to their fields for eleven.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is a God of order and His church is to be governed. The New Testament supplies two offices, elder and deacon, with stated qualifications, and a plurality of elders as the pattern. The regulative principle in worship and the ordered courses of David's realm rest on the same conviction: what God appoints, He appoints in detail, and the detail is mercy.

pos: n. pl. (the inhabitants of the country east of the sea of Galilee where Christ cast out the legion)
etymology: Greek Gergesenon, of Gergesa, a town on the eastern shore of the sea of Galilee; named once, Matthew 8:28.
biblical_def: The Gergesenes are the people of the country in which Christ met the demoniacs: “And when he was come to the other side into the country of the Gergesenes, there met him two possessed with devils, coming out of the tombs, exceeding fierce, so that no man might pass by that way” (Matthew 8:28). Mark and Luke call the same district the country of the Gadarenes, naming it from the larger city of Gadara, while Matthew names it from the nearer town on the shore. The devils confessed Him on sight: “And, behold, they cried out, saying, What have we to do with thee, Jesus, thou Son of God? art thou come hither to torment us before the time?” (Matthew 8:29). They begged to enter the swine, were permitted, and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea and perished in the waters. The country was Gentile, which is why there were swine in it at all, and the men of the place asked Him to depart. It is one of the plainest demonstrations in the Gospels of Christ's absolute authority over the powers of darkness, rendered in front of a herd of pigs and a town that preferred its commerce.

corruption_summary: Demon possession is reinterpreted as ancient language for mental illness; the narrative turns on devils who confess Christ's deity, bargain, and enter animals.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard liberal handling of this account converts the demoniacs into psychiatric patients and the devils into a first-century idiom. The text will not carry it. The spirits address Jesus by His divine title before anyone else in Matthew has done so, ask whether He has come to torment them before the time — a statement of eschatology, not of symptom — negotiate their destination, and then demonstrably move into a herd of swine that drowns. A delusion does not relocate into two thousand pigs.

The second corruption is the opposite excess: a fascination with the demonic that makes the devil the main subject. Matthew's interest is Christ's authority. He speaks one word, Go, and the matter is settled. The townspeople's response is the warning in the passage — they came out to meet Him and besought Him to depart out of their coasts, having counted the cost of His presence in pigs. Christ left, and the country kept its swine.

pos: n. pl. (the men of Athens, before whom Paul preached on Mars' hill)
etymology: Greek Athenaioi, men of Athens, from Athenai, the city named for its tutelary goddess; named once, Acts 17:21.
biblical_def: The Athenians are described in a parenthesis that is one of the sharpest sentences in the Acts: “(For all the Athenians and strangers which were there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell, or to hear some new thing.)” (Acts 17:21). Luke sets it immediately before Paul's address, and it frames everything that follows. The city was the intellectual capital of the ancient world, full of philosophers, and Luke characterises its whole occupation as the consumption of novelty. Paul's sermon meets them exactly there: “Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious” (Acts 17:22). He preaches the God who made the world and all things therein, who is not worshipped with men's hands, who made of one blood all nations, and who has appointed a day of judgment by a Man He raised from the dead. He closes with the demand the Athenians had no category for: “And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent” (Acts 17:30). Some mocked, some deferred, and certain men believed, Dionysius the Areopagite among them.

corruption_summary: Paul at Athens is held up as the model of accommodating the gospel to the culture; he quoted a poet in one clause and commanded universal repentance in the next.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 17 is the most abused missionary text in the New Testament. It is regularly produced to justify a preaching that begins and ends with the hearer's own categories — find the altar to the unknown god, quote the local poets, affirm the search. Paul does begin there, and then he dismantles the whole edifice: the God who made the world does not dwell in temples made with hands, is not served by human hands as though He needed anything, has made every nation of one blood, and now commands all men everywhere to repent because He has appointed a day of judgment. Contact with the culture was the doorway; the content was creation, judgment, repentance and resurrection.

The second corruption is intellectualism, and Athens is its portrait. A city of unrivalled learning spent its time telling and hearing some new thing, and when it heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked and others said they would hear again of the matter. Novelty is not inquiry. The men who believed that day believed a scandal that their philosophy had no room for, and the LORD added them to the church anyway.

pos: n. pl. (the inhabitants of Damascus, in Paul's account of his escape)
etymology: Greek Damaskenon, of Damascus, from the Hebrew Dammeseq; named once, 2 Corinthians 11:32.
biblical_def: The Damascenes are named once, in the last item of Paul's catalogue of sufferings: “In Damascus the governor under Aretas the king kept the city of the Damascenes with a garrison, desirous to apprehend me” (2 Corinthians 11:32). The escape follows: “And through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands” (2 Corinthians 11:33). Paul has just finished listing stripes, prisons, shipwrecks, perils of waters, of robbers, of his own countrymen, of false brethren — and he ends the list, deliberately, with the least heroic thing in it. He was lowered out of a window in a laundry basket. The context is his answer to the boasters who had unsettled Corinth: if he must glory, he will glory in his infirmities, because the Lord had told him that strength is made perfect in weakness. Damascus was where he had been struck blind and where he first preached Christ in the synagogues, and it was the first city he had to flee. The governor under Aretas held the gates against one man, and the LORD took that man out over the wall in a basket.

corruption_summary: Apostolic authority is imagined as triumphalist power; Paul establishes his by listing beatings and an undignified escape in a basket.
corruption_paragraphs: The health-and-prosperity reading of the apostolic ministry cannot survive 2 Corinthians 11. Challenged by men who commended themselves, Paul answers with a list of what has been done to him, and he caps it with the window and the basket. Then he gives the reason: the Lord said, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. The modern substitute — authority proved by success, visible blessing as the mark of God's favour — is the precise error the chapter was written against.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's power is displayed through the weakness of His servants, and that this is not a consolation prize but the design. The one city named for its people in this list is Damascus, the city of Paul's conversion and his first flight. Where he was blinded he was also hunted, and he counted both among the things in which he would glory.

pos: n. pl. (a people in Shishak's army against Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Sukkiyim, dwellers in tents or booths, from sukkah, a booth; named once, 2 Chronicles 12:3.
biblical_def: The Sukkiims are one of three peoples named in the host Shishak brought against Jerusalem: “With twelve hundred chariots, and threescore thousand horsemen: and the people were without number that came with him out of Egypt; the Lubims, the Sukkiims, and the Ethiopians” (2 Chronicles 12:3). The name means men of the booths, and they are generally taken for a nomadic or tent-dwelling people of the African desert serving in the Egyptian army. The cause of the invasion is stated without ambiguity in the previous verse: “And it came to pass, that in the fifth year of king Rehoboam Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem, because they had transgressed against the LORD” (2 Chronicles 12:2). The chapter is one of Scripture's clearest cases of a foreign army as the rod of God's chastisement on His own people. Shemaiah the prophet told the princes of Judah plainly, Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak; and when they humbled themselves the LORD granted them deliverance, though not escape — Shishak took the treasures of the house of the LORD, and Rehoboam made shields of brass to replace Solomon's gold.

scriptures: With twelve hundred chariots, and threescore thousand horsemen: and the people were without number that came with him out of Egypt; the Lubims, the Sukkiims, and the Ethiopians.
And it came to pass, that in the fifth year of king Rehoboam Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem, because they had transgressed against the LORD,

Then came Shemaiah the prophet to Rehoboam, and to the princes of Judah, that were gathered together to Jerusalem because of Shishak, and said unto them, Thus saith the LORD, Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak.

So Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem, and took away the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king's house; he took all: he carried away also the shields of gold which Solomon had made.
corruption_summary: National calamity is read as politics only; Chronicles names the invasion as the LORD's chastisement for Judah's transgression, with the prophet's word attached.
corruption_paragraphs: Secular history reads Shishak's campaign as an Egyptian reassertion of influence in the Levant, and so it was. Chronicles does not deny the politics; it supplies the cause. Judah had transgressed against the LORD, and the LORD left them in the hand of Shishak. The modern refusal to read providence in national events is not neutrality but a prior commitment, and it leaves the reader unable to take the chapter at its word.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God governs the armies of the nations and uses them to chastise His own people, and that humbling is the appointed response. The princes of Judah said, The LORD is righteous, and the sentence of destruction was lifted while the loss remained. Solomon's gold went to Egypt and brass took its place in the house of God — a standing picture of what sin costs a church even after it repents.

pos: n. pl. (a people descended from Dedan, son of Jokshan, by Keturah)
etymology: Hebrew Le'ummim, peoples, or nations, from le'om, a people; named once, Genesis 25:3.
biblical_def: The Leummim are the last of the three peoples sprung from Dedan in the line of Abraham by Keturah: “And Jokshan begat Sheba, and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were Asshurim, and Letushim, and Leummim” (Genesis 25:3). The line begins in the verse that opens the chapter: “Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah” (Genesis 25:1). These are Abraham's children too, and the register of them is one of the quiet proofs of the promise that he should be a father of many nations. The name means simply peoples. They are not heard of again, and they have no part in the covenant line, which the next verses settle plainly: Abraham gave gifts to the sons of the concubines and sent them away eastward, and “Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac” (Genesis 25:5). The sorting is deliberate and it is the pattern of election. Many came out of Abraham; one line carried the promise. Paul builds the argument of Romans 9 on exactly this: they are not all children of Abraham that are of his seed, for in Isaac shall thy seed be called.

corruption_summary: Election is softened into God's general goodwill toward all; Genesis 25 shows Abraham's many sons sent away with gifts and the promise given to one.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of election is nowhere more plainly illustrated than in the household of Abraham, and nowhere more consistently avoided. Abraham fathered Ishmael, then Isaac, then six sons by Keturah with peoples descending from them — Leummim among those grandchildren. All were his seed. One line received the covenant. Scripture states the division without apology: the sons of the concubines received gifts and were sent eastward, and Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac.

Paul takes up this very history to answer the objection that God's word had failed: neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children; but, In Isaac shall thy seed be called. Unconditional election is therefore not a late Reformed imposition on the text but the argument the apostle draws out of Genesis. The Leummim are a nation that came of Abraham and never heard the promise, and their existence in the register is part of how Scripture teaches that the promise is God's to place.
